1.o: In this chapter we have Naomi's afflictions. I. As a distressed housekeeper, forced by famine to remove into the land of Moab, ver. 1, 2. II. As a mournful widow and mother, bewailing the death of her husband and her two sons, ver. 3-5. III. As a careful mother-in-law, desirous to be kind to her two daughters, but at a loss how to be so when she returns to her own country, ver. 6-13. Orpah she parts with in sorrow, ver. 14. Ruth she takes with her in fear, ver. 15-18. IV.
1.i: After her husband and sons die in Moab, Naomi returns to Bethlehem, and Ruth the Moabite refuses to leave her.
1.p: Lord, You are the God of those who are loyal and loving. Make us faithful friends. Amen.
1.l: Tell someone today you will stick with them in a hard time, and mean it.
q: Ruth chose Naomi and Naomi's God. Who has chosen to stick with you, and who can you stick with?

2.o: There is scarcely any chapter in all the sacred history that stoops so low as this to take cognizance of so mean a person as Ruth, a poor Moabitish widow, so mean an action as her gleaning corn in a neighbour's field, and the minute circumstances thereof. But all this was in order to her being grafted into the line of Christ and taken in among his ancestors, that she might be a figure of the espousals of the Gentile church to Christ, Isa. liv. 1.
2.i: Ruth gleaned grain in the field of Boaz, who noticed her loyalty to Naomi, protected her, fed her, and told his workers to leave extra for her.
2.p: Lord, You provide for the poor and the stranger. Make us faithful workers and generous neighbors. Amen.
2.l: Be kind to a newcomer or someone who is new in your class or neighborhood today. Ask their name, and invite them in.
q: Not every branch of the tree is a top branch. Which relative of yours is poor, and what do you owe them?

3.o: We found it very easy, in the former chapter, to applaud the decency of Ruth's behaviour, and to show what good use we may make of the account given us of it; but in this chapter we shall have much ado to vindicate it from the imputation of indecency, and to save it from having an ill use made of it; but the goodness of those times was such as saved what is recorded here from being ill done, and yet the badness of these times is such as that it will not justify any now in doing the like. Here is, I.
3.i: On Naomi's advice, Ruth asks Boaz to act as her family redeemer, and Boaz promises to settle the matter.
3.p: Lord, You are a redeemer. Give us patience to wait while You work things out. Amen.
3.l: Do a quiet kindness today that no one will know about, and trust God to see it.
q: Ruth did what Naomi said, and then waited. Is it harder for you to act or to wait?

4.o: In this chapter we have the wedding between Boaz and Ruth, in the circumstances of which there was something uncommon, which is kept upon record for the illustration, not only of the law concerning the marrying of a brother's widow (Deut. xxv. 5, &c.), for cases help to expound laws, but of the gospel too, for from this marriage descended David, and the Son of David, whose espousals to the Gentile church were hereby typified. We are here told, I. How Boaz got clear of his rival, and fairly shook him off, ver. 1-8.
4.i: Boaz redeemed Naomi's land and married Ruth before the town elders, and their son Obed became the grandfather of King David.
4.p: Lord, You are our redeemer. Thank You for bringing outsiders into Your family, and for keeping Your promises across generations. Amen.
4.l: Make a promise to someone today and keep it, big or small, so they can count on you.
q: Boaz did the right thing in public. Where are you tempted to take a shortcut in private?
